bullets.t: This is the Second Pylon, the grand gateway to the Great Hypostyle Hall, built by Horemheb, who ruled from 1323 to 1295 BC. Its core is packed with blocks from Akhenaten's demolished temples.
The giant beside the doorway is Ramesses II, with his tiny daughter Bent'anta between his feet. Digital Karnak records it as Nineteenth Dynasty sandstone, not granite as some captions say.
Ramesses VI and, later, Pinedjem I, a High Priest of Amun who ruled Thebes as a king about 1054 BC, each had their names cut into this statue. Reusing monuments was common at Karnak.

This gateway nearly fell in 1899. Collapsing hall columns struck it, stones dropped and a wall bulged. Engineers propped it with timber, sandbags, an 11-metre buttress and cement poured into the cracks.
The carved passage through the pylon was begun by Ramesses I, who reigned under two years. Ramesses II recut it in sunk relief, and faint traces of the older raised carving still show.
In Horemheb's day this was the temple's front door. The shrines of Sety II and Ramesses III, and then Shoshenq I's great court, were added in front of it over the next 350 years.
If a painting in a Theban tomb is read correctly, a T-shaped harbour basin joined to the Nile lay near here, and Horemheb's builders filled it in first. That reading is an interpretation, not proof.

kids.t: Find the tiny princess standing between the giant king's feet!

pylon2.look: The sandstone colossus of Ramesses II with a small princess at his feet, standing in front of the pylon beside the doorway into the Hypostyle Hall.
pylon2.note: This doorway is the usual way into the Hypostyle Hall, and no closure was reported in visitor accounts up to December 2025. The statue is sandstone, not granite.

bullets.t: You are in the Great Hypostyle Hall: 134 sandstone columns in a space about 103 metres wide and 52 deep. Sety I began it about 1294 BC, and his son Ramesses II finished it.
Sources vary, but the twelve centre columns are about 20 metres high, the other 122 about 12 to 15. Each flower top is 5.4 metres across, said to hold a hundred people.
Look up at the stone window grilles. The centre columns are taller, so the roof steps up, and the gap holds windows. Their shafts of light once lit a dim, roofed forest of columns.
There were no cranes. Builders buried each course of stone in earth and mud-brick ramps, dragged the next stones up, and removed the earth only at the end, smoothing the walls from the top down.
Look for the horizontal joints on a column: each is a stack of drums or half-drums, some about five tons. The sandstone probably came by barge from Gebel el-Silsila, about 160 kilometres south.

On 3 October 1899 eleven north-wing columns fell in a chain reaction, the crash reportedly heard at Luxor Temple. Foundations of small reused blocks, crumbling in salty groundwater, could not carry the load.

Georges Legrain rebuilt them. He banked earth round a column to lift a pulley, took it down in half-drums, rebuilt the north half on new foundations and underpinned the south with brick, finishing in 1902.
Since 2021 conservators have cleaned the columns of sand, dust and bird debris, revealing paint and carved detail. In January 2024 the antiquities council said 95 per cent were done.
Digital Karnak, a website with a 3D model begun at UCLA and now hosted at UC Santa Cruz, rebuilds this hall with its roof on, much darker than today. It leaves out the carvings.

kids.t: Look way up high: can you spot the stone windows with bars?
Find the biggest flower-shaped tops on the tall middle columns!

kids: Find a column with a king carved on it, standing tall next to a god.
hypostyle.look: 134 giant columns; walk the central aisle first, then look up at the stone window grilles high on the sides.
hypostyle.note: Open on the main ticket: visitor accounts from October and December 2025 show it open, and cleaning of 95 per cent of the columns was reported complete in January 2024. Busiest from about 09:00 to 10:00 when tour buses arrive; the side aisles are partly open to the sky, so shade is patchy.

bullets.t: On this outer wall Sety I's sculptors carved his wars: the king charging alone in his chariot against enemies in Canaan, Lebanon, Syria and Libya. They date from about 1290 BC.
The wall is a mirror image on both sides of the doorway, in three rows. East, on your left as you face it, is his first-year campaign through Sinai and Canaan; west are later wars.
On the west half, Kadesh is attacked at the top, Libyans are beaten in the middle and Hittites below. The Libyan scene, the best preserved, shows Sety spearing a chief from his chariot.

The king always wins alone; no Egyptian army appears. A small figure behind him is labelled Crown Prince Ramesses, but underneath is the name of an officer, Mehy, replaced by Ramesses II, for reasons unknown.
This is royal propaganda, but historians use it: the scenes show the fortified road across Sinai, the cedars of Lebanon and Egypt's war with the Hittites, before Ramesses II's peace treaty.
Salt-laden groundwater is eating the lower stone. Chicago's Epigraphic Survey copied these scenes in the 1970s and 1980s, a record more valuable now, as the carving keeps decaying.
Out here the war scenes are in bold sunk relief. Inside the hall, Sety's carvers used finer raised relief, which took longer to cut.

kids.t: Find the king's horses and the big round wheel of his chariot!

northwall.look: Outside the north wall of the Hypostyle Hall: Sety I in his chariot charging through his enemies, carved across the whole wall.
northwall.note: Reached by the path along the outside of the north wall. December 2025 photographs show the foot of the wall reachable and no closure was reported, but no review mentions it, so it may be roped off; if so, skip it and spend the time in the hall. The wall faces north, so in March it is in shade all day and the carving reads softly, not in raking light.
